claim: Abnormal connectivity patterns exist between resting state networks in neuropsychiatric disorders, including Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD).
source: The existence of abnormal connectivity patterns between resting state networks in neuropsychiatric disorders, including Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), has been well established.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract, drawing on existing scientific consensus.

claim: Traditional treatment methods in ASD are limited and do not address aberrant network structure.
source: Traditional treatment methods in ASD are limited, and do not address the aberrant network structure.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation in the abstract, drawing on established understanding of ASD treatments.

claim: Real-time fMRI neurofeedback training produced large, significant long-term changes in correlations at the network level in participants with ASD.
source: This training regimen produced large, significant long-term changes in correlations at the network level, and whole brain analysis revealed that the greatest changes were focused on the areas being trained.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including Figure 3 showing changes across training days.

claim: The greatest changes in connectivity were focused on the areas being trained.
source: This training regimen produced large, significant long-term changes in correlations at the network level, and whole brain analysis revealed that the greatest changes were focused on the areas being trained.
evidence: This is supported by whole brain analysis data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Changes in connectivity were not found in the control group.
source: These changes were not found in the control group.
evidence: This is supported by data comparing ASD and TD groups shown in Figure 4.

claim: Changes in ASD resting state connectivity following training were correlated to changes in behavior.
source: Moreover, changes in ASD resting state connectivity following the training were correlated to changes in behavior, suggesting that neurofeedback can be used to directly alter complex, clinically relevant network connectivity patterns.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between connectivity changes and SRS scores shown in Figure 7.

claim: Behavioral treatment options for ASD are limited in their efficacy and often do not generalize well beyond the specific training paradigm.
source: Behavioural treatment options are limited in their efficacy, and often do not generalize well beyond the specific training paradigm (Otero et al., 2015; Williams White et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Numerous studies have documented widespread patterns of aberrant brain functional connectivity in patients with ASD, involving many cortical regions including frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes.
source: Numerous studies have documented widespread patterns of aberrant brain functional connectivity in patients with ASD, involving many cortical regions including frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes (Müller et al., 2011; Picci et al., 2016; Di Martino et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Multiple cortical areas are significantly under-connected in patients with ASD compared to typically developing control subjects.
source: Specifically, these studies show that multiple cortical areas are significantly under-connected in patients with ASD compared to typically developing (TD) control subjects, although over-connectivity has also been reported (Hahamy et al., 2015; Belmonte et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The degree of diminished connectivity in ASD was found to be correlated with symptom severity.
source: At the individual level, the degree of diminished connectivity as well as measures of cortical thickness were found to be correlated with symptom severity (Gotts et al., 2012; Wallace et al., 2012; Di Martino et al., 2009b; Assaf et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Connectivity measures were predictive of future progression of autistic symptoms.
source: and this measure of connectivity was even predictive of future progression of autistic symptoms (Plitt et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: There is a causal link between connectivity and behavior in ASD, such that changing the connectivity might lead to a change in behavior.
source: Together, these findings suggest a causal link between connectivity and behavior, such that changing the connectivity might lead to a change in behavior.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited literature and the study's rationale.

claim: Traditional, explicit training paradigms activate aberrant networks in ASD, potentially reinforcing sub-optimal connectivity.
source: Traditional, explicit training paradigms, activate these aberrant networks (Kana et al., 2009; Di Martino et al., 2009a), thus potentially reinforcing the sub-optimal connectivity.
evidence: This claim combines cited evidence with inference about the potential negative effects.

claim: Real-time fMRI neurofeedback is an emerging technique with great potential for clinical applications.
source: Real-time fMRI neurofeedback (rt-fMRI-nf) is an emerging technique with great potential for clinical applications (Stoeckel et al., 2014; Sulzer et al., 2013; Weiskopf, 2012; Birbaumer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Covert neurofeedback is a variant of neurofeedback in which participants are given no strategy to control the feedback and might not be cognizant that the feedback is related to brain activity.
source: Covert neurofeedback is a variant of neurofeedback, in which participants are given no strategy with which to control the feedback, and might not even be cognizant that the feedback is related to brain activity.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the manuscript.

claim: Positive and negative reinforcement of brain activity patterns are sufficient for promoting small but widespread changes in network connectivity, even without any learning intention on the part of participants.
source: This decision is motivated by recent work showing that positive and negative reinforcement of brain activity patterns are sufficient for promoting small but widespread changes in network connectivity, even without any learning intention on the part of participants (Ramot et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Multi-voxel pattern analysis (MVPA) techniques have been successful at training complex patterns of activity within a given network.
source: A number of studies have been successful at training complex patterns of activity within a given network using multi-voxel pattern analysis (MVPA) techniques (deBettencourt et al., 2015; Amano et al., 2016; Shibata et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Feedback-related changes correspond to robust behavioral changes after only a few sessions, with significant change being detectable after as little as one training session.
source: with feedback related changes corresponding to robust behavioural changes after only a few sessions, and significant change being detectable after as little as one training session.
evidence: This claim is based on the cited MVPA neurofeedback studies.

claim: Feedback-induced behavioral changes range from very local and low level (such as changes in perception of line orientation after V1 training) to changes in high level functions such as attention and fear perception.
source: Feedback induced behavioural changes have been shown to range from very local and low level, such as changes in perception of line orientation after V1 training (Shibata et al., 2011), or inducing color association in V1 in a somewhat less local paradigm (Amano et al., 2016), to changes in high level functions such as attention (deBettencourt et al., 2015), and fear perception (Koizumi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Neurofeedback-induced changes can be bi-directional, both behaviorally and at the network level.
source: Such changes can even be bi-directional, both behaviourally and at the network level (Cortese et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: 17 ASD participants and 10 control participants were scanned over multiple sessions (123 sessions in total).
source: 17 ASD participants and 10 control participants were scanned over multiple sessions (123 sessions in total).
evidence: This is a description of the study design and participant numbers.

claim: Target1 in superior temporal sulcus (STS) and target2 in somatosensory cortex showed large under-connectivity in ASD compared with TD individuals.
source: We used previously collected resting state data on large groups of ASD and TD participants (N = 56 ASD, 62 TD) to identify two target brain regions that showed large under-connectivity in ASD compared with TD individuals, while also being physically distant from each other, and belonging to separate networks (Figure 1): target1 in superior temporal sulcus (STS) and target2 in somatosensory cortex
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of previously collected data shown in Figure 1.

claim: STS and somatosensory cortex have been consistently implicated in social processing.
source: both of which have been consistently implicated in social processing (Allison et al., 2000; Frith and Frith, 2010; Adolphs, 2009; Damasio et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: STS and somatosensory cortex have previously been found to be under-connected and atypically activated in ASD.
source: and have previously been found to be under-connected and atypically activated in ASD (Chen et al., 2015; Gotts et al., 2012; Müller et al., 2001; Tuttle et al., 2016; Khan et al., 2015; Khan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Under-connectivity between STS and somatosensory networks in ASD was significant in both the large dataset (p<4.3×10−5) and in the 17 participants recruited for the neurofeedback study (p=0.002).
source: As in the previously published subset of the dataset, we found that under-connectivity between these two networks (STS and somatosensory) in ASD was significant in both this large dataset (p<4.3×10−5) and in the 17 participants recruited for the neurofeedback study (p=0.002)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Under-connectivity between STS and somatosensory networks was significantly correlated to social symptom severity as measured by the Social Responsiveness Scale (SRS).
source: as well as significantly correlated to social symptom severity, as measured by the Social Responsiveness Scale (SRS) (r = −0.35 p<0.009 without regressors, r = −0.31, p<0.026, using age and motion as regressors, r values represent Pearson's correlation, p-values determined by permutation tests).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of connectivity and behavioral measures.

claim: The SRS is a parent-filled questionnaire designed to be a continuous, cardinal measure of social symptom severity in ASD.
source: The SRS is a parent filled questionnaire, which is designed to be a continuous, cardinal measure of social symptom severity in ASD, and has been shown to correlate with functional brain connectivity measures in multiple studies (Anderson et al., 2011; Di Martino et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is a description of the SRS measure supported by citations.

claim: The lower the connectivity between STS and somatosensory networks, the more severe the social symptoms (higher score on the SRS).
source: This result indicates that connectivity between these two networks is clinically relevant, i.e. the lower the connectivity, the more severe the social symptoms (higher score on the SRS).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation data presented.

claim: IPL was significantly over-correlated to STS target1 in the ASD cohort participating in this study.
source: IPL was significantly over-correlated to STS target1 in the ASD cohort participating in this study (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The combination of under-connectivity between STS and somatosensory with over-connectivity to the default mode network is in line with recent evidence of reduced within-network cohesion coupled with reduced between-network differentiation in ASD.
source: This combination of under-connectivity between STS and somatosensory with over-connectivity to the default mode network, is in line with recent evidence of reduced within-network cohesion coupled with reduced between-network differentiation (Hahamy et al., 2015; Keown et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim connects the study findings to previous research through citations.

claim: The composite difference measure was significantly different between the ASD group and the TD group in both the previous large dataset (p=0.001) and in the current cohort (p<1×10−4).
source: This measure was also significantly different between the ASD group and the TD group in both the previous large dataset (p=0.001), and in our cohort (p<1×10−4), Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: 17 patients with ASD participated in four training sessions over the course of 8 days.
source: For the initial part of the study, 17 patients with ASD participated in four training sessions, over the course of 8 days (two sessions of two consecutive days each, a week apart).
evidence: This describes the study design and participant numbers.

claim: Each training session consisted of two rest scans, followed by four neurofeedback training scans, and finally two more rest scans.
source: Each session consisted of two rest scans, followed by four neurofeedback training scans, and finally two more rest scans (Each scan was 9 min in duration. See Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol shown in Figure 2.

claim: 15 of the 17 original participants returned for a follow-up study.
source: An additional follow up study was then carried out, in which 15 of the 17 original participants returned for a final, slightly shorter training session.
evidence: This describes the follow-up study design.

claim: The interval between the original training and the follow-up varied greatly between subjects, ranging from 5 to 56 weeks.
source: The interval between the original training and the follow up varied greatly between subjects, and ranged from 5 to 56 weeks.
evidence: This describes the temporal design of the follow-up study.

claim: The 'two-point' method was validated as being a good proxy for correlation analysis by comparing results to standard Pearson's correlation offline (r = 0.61, p<1×10−4).
source: This 'two-point' method was validated as being a good proxy for correlation analysis by comparing the results from this to standard Pearson's correlation offline (r = 0.61, p<1×10−4 permutation test, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by validation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Participants were blind to the purpose of the study, the mechanism of the neurofeedback, and even to the fact that it was neurofeedback.
source: Participants were blind to the purpose of the study, as well as to the mechanism of the neurofeedback, and even to the fact that it was neurofeedback.
evidence: This describes the blinding procedure, confirmed by exit questionnaires in Table 1.

claim: None of the participants' reported strategies held any resemblance to the neurofeedback algorithm.
source: Responses as to the perceived nature of the 'puzzle task' varied widely, as did reported strategies, but none held any resemblance to the neurofeedback algorithm.
evidence: This is based on analysis of exit questionnaire responses shown in Table 1.

claim: Most participants were highly motivated to solve the puzzles, with only 3 of 11 participants reporting a motivation score of less than 5 on a scale of 1-10.
source: Despite not knowing what they were supposed to do, most participants were highly motivated to solve the puzzles, with only 3 of the 11 participants for which responses are available reporting a motivation score of less than 5 (on a scale of 1–10, see Table 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of exit questionnaire responses shown in Table 1.

claim: An additional control group of 10 TD participants completed the same initial 4 day training regimen following the same protocol as the ASD group.
source: An additional control group of 10 TD participants completed the same initial 4 day training regimen, following the same protocol as the above.
evidence: This describes the control group design.

claim: The TD control group received feedback on the same three nodes but in a different network configuration, with target1 in STS remaining the same but somatosensory target2 and IPL control region switching roles.
source: This group received feedback on the same three nodes, but in a different network configuration: target1 in the STS remained the same, but somatosensory target2 and the IPL control region switched roles, so that feedback was given whenever STS (target1) and IPL (now target2) were co-modulated, and were opposite to somatosensory cortex (now control), see Figure 2—figure supplement 3.
evidence: This describes the control group protocol shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The feedback given to the TD control group was antithetical to the normal connectivity patterns found in the typically developing brain.
source: Another key difference is that this feedback was antithetical to the normal connectivity patterns found in the typically developing brain, as STS and somatosensory are well correlated in the typically developing brain, whereas the IPL region used in this study was explicitly chosen to be as uncorrelated as possible with STS in TDs during rest (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is based on the connectivity patterns shown in Figure 1 and the experimental design.

claim: Over the course of the four training days, correlations between the two target regions steadily increased in the ASD group, with a significant difference between day1 and day4 (p=4×10−4, mean change in correlation = 0.11).
source: As can be seen, over the course of the four training days, correlations between the two target regions steadily increased (with a significant difference between most days, p=4×10−4 between day1 and day4, mean change in correlation = 0.11, Figure 3A)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Correlations between target1 and control decreased in the ASD group, with a significant difference between day1 and day4 (p=8×10−4, mean change = −0.13).
source: while correlations between target1 and control decreased (significant difference between day1 and all other days, p=8×10−4 between day1 and day4 mean change = −0.13, Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was a strong and consistent increase in the composite difference measure between day1 and day4 in the ASD group (p<2×10−4, mean change = 0.19).
source: Figure 3D shows the overall composite difference measure, taking into account all three correlation pairs, where there is a strong and consistent increase between day1 and day4 (p<2×10−4, mean change = 0.19).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 15 of the 17 ASD participants showed a positive change in the composite difference measure from day1 to day4.
source: 15 of the 17 participants showed a positive change in this measure (14/17 had a positive change in target1-target2 correlations, as well as a negative change in target1-control correlations).
evidence: This is based on individual participant data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The TD control group showed no significant changes between days in any of the three pairwise combinations or in the composite difference measure.
source: The TD control group on the other hand, showed no significant changes between days in any of the three pairwise combinations, or in the composite difference measure.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the TD control group data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Only 4/10 participants in the TD control group showed a change in the trained direction in the composite measure, within the range of chance.
source: Only 4/10 participants in this group showed a change in the trained direction in the composite measure, within the range of chance, and the magnitude of change was minimal relative to the change seen in the ASD participants.
evidence: This is based on analysis of individual TD participant data shown in Figure 4.

claim: A significant difference (p=9.2×10−4) was found between the learning seen in the TD and ASD groups in a two-sample t-test comparing the change in composite correlations.
source: A significant difference (p=9.2×10−4) was found between the learning seen in the TD and ASD groups in this analysis.
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison between the two groups.

claim: The learning in the ASD group was mostly, though not fully, preserved even after an extended time period of 5-56 weeks.
source: Our results indicate that the learning was mostly, though not fully, preserved, even after such an extended time period (Figure 3A–D, follow up).
evidence: This claim is supported by follow-up data shown in Figure 3.

claim: There was no correlation between the time that had elapsed and the rate of retention of learning.
source: In fact, although there was variation between subjects in the degree of retention, there was no correlation between the time that had elapsed and the rate of retention (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The strongest positive change in correlation to target1 over the training period was in the somatosensory cortex (with a peak at target2), and the strongest negative change was in the control region.
source: The changes were exactly as predicted by the training: the strongest positive change in correlation to target1 over the training period was in the somatosensory cortex (with a peak at target2), and the strongest negative change was in the control region.
evidence: This is based on whole brain analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Changes to correlations with target2 were seen in the STS with a peak in target1, and negative changes in correlation to control were seen in bilateral STS.
source: Changes to correlations with target2 were seen in the STS with a peak in target1, and negative changes in correlation to control were seen in bilateral STS (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole brain analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Using target1 relative to the control seed, the largest change in the whole brain was found in target2, even though that region was not pre-selected.
source: These results support a causative role for the feedback itself, as the specific relationship that was trained between the two targets and the control came up in completely independent, whole-brain analysis. That is, using target1 relative to the control seed, the largest change in the whole brain was found in target2, even though that region was not pre-selected and the analyses did not constrain this to happen, and vice-versa using target2 and control.
evidence: This is based on whole brain analysis shown in Figure 5 and supports a causal interpretation.

claim: No significant peaks were identified in any of the target or control regions for the TD control group in the whole brain analysis.
source: Note that Figure 5 shows results only for the ASD group, as no significant peaks were identified in any of the target or control regions for the TD control group, and no voxels survived the cluster correction threshold.
evidence: This describes the null result for the TD control group in whole brain analysis.

claim: The peaks of connectivity changes were centered on the regions being trained, but the changes spread to entire networks.
source: However, it is important to note in this regard that though the peaks were centered on the regions we were training, the changes spread to entire networks, as would be expected from the architecture of the brain, which is composed of large-scale networks of multiple brain regions, making it difficult to induce changes to just one region in isolation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the whole brain analysis results shown in Figure 5.

claim: It is possible to train networks that are fundamentally connected, but it is much more difficult to train networks that are uncorrelated or weakly correlated in the typically developing brain.
source: In a larger context, the failure to induce change in the direction of training in the control subjects, suggests that while it is possible to train networks that are fundamentally connected, it is much more difficult to train networks that are uncorrelated or weakly correlated in the typically developing brain.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential results between ASD and TD groups.

claim: Some networks may be more difficult to train than others.
source: It is also possible that some networks may be more difficult to train than others, as has previously been suggested (Harmelech et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Significant changes in resting state connectivity were found between day1 and the follow-up (target1-target2 mean change = 0.09, p<0.011; composite correlations measure mean change = 0.11, p<2×10−4).
source: and between day1 and the follow up (target1-target2 mean change = 0.09, p<0.011, composite correlations measure mean change = 0.11, p<2×10−4).
evidence: This claim is supported by follow-up resting state analysis data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Change in resting state connectivity was significantly correlated to change during the neurofeedback scans (r = 0.42, p<0.04).
source: Change in rest was significantly correlated to change during the neurofeedback scans (r = 0.42, p<0.04, permutation test).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between rest and training data.

claim: 14/15 participants who came in for the follow-up showed an increase in the composite correlation measure.
source: Moreover, 14/15 participants who came in for the follow up showed an increase in the composite correlation measure (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by individual participant data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There was no significant change in connectivity for any of the pairwise correlations or the composite correlation measure in 19 ASD participants who had two resting state scans from different time points (average time between sessions 13.2 months) from a previous study.
source: 19 participants had two such data points, and the average time between the sessions was 13.2 months. The change however was not significant for any of the pairwise correlations, or the composite correlation measure (Figure 6A).
evidence: This control analysis shown in Figure 6A demonstrates that time alone does not produce connectivity changes.

claim: There was no significant change in connectivity from the previous experiment to day1 before training (mean time interval = 38.3 months, mean change = −0.04) in 10 participants who had data from both studies.
source: While there was no significant change from the previous experiment to day1 (mean time interval = 38.3 months, mean change = −0.04)
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There was significant change in connectivity from the previous experiment to day4 (mean change = 0.1, p<0.019) and to the follow-up (mean change = 0.11, p<0.003) in 10 participants who had data from both studies.
source: there was significant change to day4 (mean change = 0.1, p<0.019) and to the follow up (mean change = 0.11, p<0.003).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The changes observed were not a function of elapsed time but rather occurred as a direct result of the neurofeedback regime.
source: Taken together, these analyses provide strong evidence that the changes we observed were not a function of elapsed time but rather occurred as a direct result of our neurofeedback regime.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of neurofeedback and non-neurofeedback time intervals shown in Figure 6.

claim: There was no significant change in the mean SRS score across participants, with the mean score actually slightly (though not significantly) increasing instead of decreasing as predicted.
source: Indeed, although there was no significant change in the mean SRS score across participants, with the mean score actually slightly (though not significnatly) increasing instead of decreasing as predicted (mean SRS before training = 69.8, mean SRS after training = 71.6, p=0.11)
evidence: This describes the behavioral results for the SRS measure.

claim: There was a significant correlation between changes in the resting state network and the change in SRS (r = 0.56, p=0.016).
source: there was a significant correlation between changes in the resting state network and the change in SRS (pre training minus post training, so that a positive change corresponds to a reduction in symptoms, r = 0.56, p=0.016, Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The partial correlation between change in rest vs. change in SRS, after controlling for baseline SRS and baseline rest, was higher (r = 0.62 p=0.014).
source: The partial correlation between change in rest vs. change in SRS, after controlling for baseline SRS and baseline rest, was higher (r = 0.62 p=0.014).
evidence: This claim is supported by partial correlation analysis.

claim: No correlation was found between change in BRIEF and change in resting state correlations (r = 0.09, p=0.39).
source: No such correlation was found with the BRIEF (change in SRS vs. change in resting state correlations: r = 0.56, p=0.016; change in BRIEF vs. change in resting state correlations: r = 0.09, p=0.39).
evidence: This demonstrates specificity of the behavioral correlation to the SRS measure.

claim: After removing the variance explained by the BRIEF, the correlation between rest and SRS was even higher (r = 0.6, p=0.02).
source: We further tested for the correlation between the change in SRS vs. change in the resting state correlations, after partialing out the contribution of the BRIEF. After removing the variance explained by the BRIEF, the correlation between the rest and SRS was even higher (r = 0.6, p=0.02)
evidence: This claim is supported by partial correlation analysis.

claim: Change in resting state correlations was captured by the change in SRS scores, but not the BRIEF.
source: indicating that change in resting state correlations was captured by the change in SRS scores, but not the BRIEF.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the partial correlation analysis.

claim: The SRS has consistently been shown to correlate with aberrations in network structure in ASD.
source: Note that the SRS was chosen as our behavioral measure because it has consistently been shown to correlate with aberrations in network structure in ASD (Gotts et al., 2012; Wallace et al., 2012; Di Martino et al., 2009b; Anderson et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The SRS was not designed to be used with such a short test-retest interval (3 weeks) and has only been validated for intervals of 6 months or more.
source: Nevertheless, it was not designed to be used with such a short test-retest interval (3 weeks), and has only been validated for intervals of 6 months or more (Hus et al., 2013; Constantino et al., 2003; Bölte et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: Covert neurofeedback can be used to modulate correlations between distinct, physically distant networks in the great majority of participants (15 of 17).
source: In this study, we have demonstrated that covert neurofeedback can be used to modulate correlations between distinct, physically distant networks (Figure 3), in the great majority of participants (15 of17, Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: This modulation is possible even in cases of aberrant network structure, in clinical populations, and is sustainable for extended periods of time.
source: We have further shown that this modulation is possible even in cases of aberrant network structure, in clinical populations, and is sustainable for extended periods of time (some of our follow up sessions were a year after the original training, and we saw no evidence for an effect of time as a modulator of retention, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the follow-up data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Connectivity-based neurofeedback has previously been carried out in only a handful of studies.
source: This kind of connectivity-based neurofeedback has previously been carried out in only a handful of studies (Scharnowski et al., 2014; Megumi et al., 2015; Koush et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The network approach to neurofeedback is gaining traction and shows good preliminary findings with a sound theoretical basis.
source: though the network approach to neurofeedback is gaining traction and shows not only good preliminary findings but also has a sound theoretical basis (Bassett and Khambhati, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The extraordinary specificity of the changes revealed by the whole brain analysis, peaking exactly at the small ROIs chosen for training, precludes an alternative explanation to the feedback being the cause.
source: Moreover, the extraordinary specificity of the changes revealed by the whole brain analysis (Figure 5), peaking exactly at the small ROIs that were chosen for the training, would also seem to preclude an alternative explanation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the whole brain analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The learning is spatially specific even when training disparate networks, meaning it is possible to target specific regions of the brain.
source: The further significance of the whole-brain analysis is that this learning is spatially specific even when training disparate networks, meaning that it is possible to target specific regions of the brain.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the whole brain analysis results.

claim: The failure to induce change in the direction of training in the control subjects suggests that while it is possible to train networks that are fundamentally connected, it is much more difficult to train networks that are uncorrelated or weakly correlated in the typically developing brain.
source: In a larger context, the failure to induce change in the direction of training in the control subjects, suggests that while it is possible to train networks that are fundamentally connected, it is much more difficult to train networks that are uncorrelated or weakly correlated in the typically developing brain.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential results between ASD and TD groups.

claim: The under-connectivity between the target regions chosen explains only some of the behavioral deficits and is clearly not the sole underlying cause of autism.
source: Moreover, the under-connectivity between the target regions chosen here explains only some of the behavioral deficits, and is clearly not the sole underlying cause of autism.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the approach based on knowledge of ASD.

claim: The study was designed as a proof of principle that aberrant connectivity can be addressed through neurofeedback, rather than as a clinical intervention.
source: This study was therefore designed as a proof of principle that aberrant connectivity can be addressed through neurofeedback, rather than as a clinical intervention, and whatever behavioral effects we found were expected to be modest.
evidence: This describes the study design and goals.

claim: The lack of overall mean behavioral change together with the correlation with connectivity changes makes it unlikely that the behavioral result is driven by a placebo effect.
source: The lack of overall mean change together with the correlation with connectivity changes makes it unlikely that this result is driven by a placebo effect, and on debriefing after all data were collected, it was clear that the patients and their families did not conceive of this as an intervention, and had no expectation of behavioral change following the study.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of behavioral results and debriefing data.

claim: A change in behavior following a change in connectivity suggests that functional and structural hypoconnectivity plays a causative role in ASD rather than being simply a downstream effect.
